UN warns hunger to worsen in 16 countries amid conflict, fuel costs and aid cuts
item.description:
Hunger is projected to worsen in 16 countries over the next six months, with war-hit Sudan and Yemen among five nations facing the most severe risk, United Nations food agencies warned on Friday.
The agencies cited ongoing conflicts, rising fuel prices linked to the Middle East war and sharp reductions in humanitarian assistance as key factors aggravating the situation.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and the World Food Programme (WFP) outlined the findings in their Hunger Hotspots report, which covers the period from December through May 2026.
Sudan, Yemen, South Sudan, Somalia and northern Nigeria were placed at the highest level of concern. All five countries have repeatedly appeared on the list since 2022.
The Palestinian territories were moved down one level following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza. However, 67% of Gaza’s population still faces crisis-level hunger or worse, and the report cautioned that the improvement remains fragile.
The report said the risk of famine in Sudan is expected to remain through January in 13 areas of North Darfur and South Kordofan, reports UNB.
Nearly 19.5 million people, accounting for 41% of the country’s population, faced crisis-level hunger or worse in the latest nationwide assessment.
In two displacement camps in Eastern Jebel Marra in South Darfur, acute malnutrition levels exceeded the famine threshold.
Sorghum prices in Sudan have more than doubled over the past year due to fighting and increased fuel costs associated with the Middle East conflict.
Diesel prices have also risen to more than twice their level a year ago, the report said.
Drought associated with El Niño, a natural warming of Pacific Ocean waters that affects weather patterns around the world, has further worsened the situation.
The phenomenon has affected up to 55% of cropland in Sennar state and 70% in Gedaref, two of Sudan’s major agricultural areas.
FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol told The Associated Press that drought linked to El Niño poses a serious threat to Sudan in addition to the ongoing war, further damaging food production.
In Yemen, hunger is expected to increase as fighting that resumed in July expands across several fronts, the report said.
The country has been embroiled in conflict since 2014, when Iran-backed Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene the following year.
The encirclement of Taiz in the southwest has created conditions resembling a siege, while more than 300,000 people have been displaced since the latest escalation began.
Most of the displaced people are from Taiz, Lahj and Aden provinces.
In areas controlled by the government, 1.8 million people are facing emergency levels of hunger, compared with 1.6 million in the previous assessment.
There is no recent assessment for Houthi-controlled areas, which have become increasingly difficult for aid organizations to access as the conflict intensifies.
The last nationwide projection, covering the period through February, found that 18.3 million people, or more than half of Yemen’s population, were experiencing crisis-level hunger or worse.
Bechdol said political obstacles, rather than geographical challenges, were the main barriers to reaching people in need in Yemen.
She noted that staff members of other UN agencies had been detained, while the Houthis continue to hold 73 UN staffers, including eight employees of the UN human rights office.
Yemen depends heavily on imported food and fuel, and the report warned that attacks on shipping in the Red Sea threaten this vital supply route.
Shipping has also been disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black Sea, while shipments of fertilizer from the Gulf remain largely suspended.
Humanitarian assistance has declined sharply as major donors have reduced their funding.
Food and nutrition assistance to the five countries facing the highest level of concern fell by around 62% between 2022 and 2025, with the reduction reaching 79% in Yemen.
Changes in donor governments’ priorities in recent years have removed billions of dollars from humanitarian and development funding, leaving aid agencies unable to reach as many people as before, Bechdol said.
She said predictable funding was as important as the overall amount, particularly because assistance to farmers must reach them during planting and harvesting seasons.
With El Niño forecasts available, agencies should arrange seeds in advance and take measures to protect livestock before disasters strike, rather than responding repeatedly after crises emerge, she said.
“When that window is lost, you don’t get it back,” she said. “We’re funding losses and we’re funding damage.”

item.title: Saudi strike kills 11 in Yemen
item.description:
A Saudi strike killed 11 people on Friday in Yemen, Houthi media said, as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it shot down a drone targeting Riyadh.
The latest incidents came a day after a deadly Houthi attack on a Saudi oil refinery, and add to a growing tally of violence since Yemen's civil war reignited over the summer.
The coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government against the Iran-allied Houthis, has been regularly bombing areas under their control.
In response, Houthi forces have been targeting the oil-rich kingdom almost daily, hitting energy facilities, airports and the financial district of the capital, Riyadh.
Saudi warplanes carried out a raid on a residential building in the city of Al-Turba in Taiz governorate on Friday, killing “11 citizens, most of them children,” the Houthis' Saba news agency said, citing a local source.
The agency also reported strikes targeting fuel tanks in the Saada region, the movement's birthplace and stronghold.
On Thursday, the Houthis targeted the Jazan refinery in southern Saudi Arabia, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several other people, according to the Saudi Press Agency (SPA).
The attack also triggered a fire that led to the shutdown of the facility, SPA said.
Yemen plunged back into war in July, after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the Middle East war.
Hostilities intensified in September when the Houthis, who already controlled Yemen's most densely populated areas, seized the western coastline overlooking the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait on the Red Sea.
The Houthis are now advancing toward Aden, a major southern city where the government has taken refuge after being driven out of the capital Sanaa in 2015.
Since the conflict resumed, fighting in Yemen has killed more than 2,300 people and displaced over 364,000, according to the United Nations.
Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia have killed 27 people, according to the kingdom's authorities.

item.title: Trump urges Putin to end ‘military aggression’ in Europe
item.description:
US President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Vladimir Putin to “pull back all military aggression” against Europe, in a fresh shift in tone towards the Russian leader he called his friend just last week.
Trump said he had made the request to Putin when they met in China last week, adding that he thought it would help lead to a deal to end Moscow’s grinding war in Ukraine.
Trump’s comments come a day after he hosted Nato chief Mark Rutte in Florida, after which the two leaders issued a joint statement calling on Russia not to expand the Ukraine war.
“During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe,” Trump said on his Truth Social network.
Trump said he had done so “in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly.”
“I really believe this is a strong possibility,” he added.
The statement did not specify which territories Trump meant -- and did not specifically include Ukraine, which Russia invaded in February 2022, kicking off the largest war in Europe since World War II.
European nations have been increasingly concerned by what they regard as Russian provocations, including three Russian cruise missiles landing in Nato-member Poland last week.
In their joint statement on Wednesday, Trump and Rutte said they “discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war.”
In a notable contrast with Trump’s recent criticisms of Ukraine for striking targets deep inside Russia, the US leader made no call for Kyiv to show similar restraint.
Speaking to reporters at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida on Thursday, Trump said he was unsure if Putin would be coming to the G20 summit next month in Miami, but “but if he wanted to come, he certainly can.”
Trump’s tone appeared markedly different to when Trump met Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen last week, both face-to-face and together with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Trump warmly greeted Putin and called him his “friend” at the summit, renewing concerns in Kyiv and European capitals that he was once again pivoting towards the Russian leader.
Asked Thursday about the apparent firmer tone this week, he said: “I don’t know if I was tougher. I mean, I think I’m the one that gave them the anti-tank busters, right?”
Trump often cites his approval of Javelin missile sales to Ukraine during his first term as saving the country from Russia’s initial assault.
The US envoys on the Ukraine war, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and business friend Steve Witkoff, have been accused of a similar willingness to take Moscow’s side.
In an interview with the German MD Meets Podcast on Wednesday, Kushner said that Putin had “showed restraint” because he had “agreed not to use nuclear weapons.”
Kushner also described the Russian leader, whom he has met several times, as a “grandmaster of politics” -- while calling the Ukraine conflict “a proxy war where Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia.”
But he acknowledged that the issue of territory in eastern Ukraine claimed by Moscow remained a sticking point with Putin.
“What Steve and I have deciphered from having many, many hours with President Putin and from the Russian team, is that you know the territorial issue is right now a little bit of a deadlock,” he said.
And he warned against any downward spiral in the Ukraine war, saying “it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively.”

item.title: New Zealand PM Luxon loses majority, centrists now kingmakers
item.description:
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said Friday he would reach out to an insurgent centrist party to help him stay in power, after final results from this month’s election showed his right-wing coalition had lost its parliamentary majority.
The outcome plunges the South Pacific country into weeks of political uncertainty -- and even the prospect of another election -- as it faces a grim economic forecast and rising costs of living.
Preliminary results of the November 7 poll had shown Luxon’s National Party-led coalition clinging onto power.
But margins were so tight that his party lost two seats in the final results announced Friday -- leaving his coalition with the populist NZ First and the libertarian ACT one seat short of a majority.
Luxon declared he had a mandate to form the country’s next government in the wake of this month’s vote, bitterly fought and dominated by spiraling costs of living.
He has continued running the country since the November 7 poll, but on Friday admitted that forming a new government will be “challenging.”
“I want to be upfront with New Zealanders. These negotiations may be challenging, and they could take some time,” he told journalists.
He will now need the backing of the centrist newcomers Opportunity, led by Qiulae Wong, if he wants to govern.
If a deal isn’t struck, the country could be headed for another election.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said.
“New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term.”
Pledging kinder, gentler politics as well as action on climate change, Wong’s party became the first in decades to make parliament without a former cabinet minister as leader.
She has vowed to work with whichever party has the largest number of seats.
But she has insisted that her party’s “bottom lines” on climate change action, cost of living and cleaning up politics are non-negotiable.
On the campaign trail, she ruled out working with a government in which NZ First leader Winston Peters was foreign minister, after he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your own country.”
Speaking outside parliament following the final result, she told journalists she was expecting “challenging” talks.
Wong also would not rule out taking the country to another election.
“All we can do is be as constructive and proactive as possible to make this happen. But it’s not just us around the table,” she said.
Both Luxon and opposition Labor Party leader Chris Hipkins have held lengthy meetings with Wong in the wake of the election.
Wong’s ascendancy to kingmaker in the next New Zealand government caps a remarkable rise since the 38-year-old former KPMG consultant took over the party -- polling at about one percent in August last year.
She preaches “pragmatic politics” as a counter to growing polarization, saying she wants to “bring the heat down a little bit and actually just focus on moving the country forward.”
She said following the election this month that her win represented a sea change after a decade of rising populism and extremism worldwide.
“I think we are seeing a push globally for more pragmatic politics,” she told journalists.
“We’ve seen that populism doesn’t deliver results,” she said.
With the official count in, it could take weeks or even months for the shape of New Zealand’s new government to be decided.
Following the 2023 poll, it took more than six weeks for Luxon to form his coalition government with NZ First and ACT.
In an email to supporters, NZ First told supporters Friday’s results had “not provided the certainty our country needs,” according to national broadcaster RNZ.
“Our team is ready to go so what happens over the next three months is crucial.”

item.title: Saudi pop music is thriving — but for the right reasons?
item.description:
Today, rapper Asayel Bishi is one of Saudi Arabia’s rising hip-hop stars, signed to the country’s biggest record label for new music, Mdlbeast. But not so long ago, she was making international headlines for a totally different reason.
In 2020, after Bishi released a music video for a song, “Bint Mecca,” or “girl from Mecca,” featuring people dancing in a local cafe, Mecca’s governor called for the arrest of Bishi’s whole production team. He said the video violated the holy city’s local customs and traditions. In the end, the situation was resolved with a discussion about filming permits.
And by early 2023, Bishi was signed to Mdlbeast and has since racked up hundreds of thousands of streams on music platforms like Spotify.
In the past, other Saudi rappers have ended up in prison for similar, alleged transgressions. The fact that Bishi’s story went a different way is probably partially because the 31-year-old’s career path is on a similar trajectory to the Saudi pop music industry as a whole.
As part of Saudi ruler Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 plan, announced in 2016 and which aims to move the country away from economic dependence on oil, the country has poured billions into the local music industry.
The pace of development increased in 2019 after the country held its first major festival, Soundstorm, an annual event that now draws major international acts and over 400,000 guests. Mdlbeast was created then, primarily as the festival organizer. Since then, it has also become a record label, radio station, distributor, promoter and talent incubator.
A recent report for the Saudi Music Commission suggests the music sector could be worth $500 million by 2034. But it’s difficult to figure out how well Saudi pop is really doing now because independent monitoring of the sector only began relatively recently.
Streaming platform Spotify reports that people listening to Saudi-made music inside Saudi Arabia increased by 195% between 2020 and 2024. However, the most-streamed artists inside the country are still international.
Although there was a mostly-hidden Saudi music scene before this recent boom, observers say the growth of the Saudi music sector is not organic.
It’s all about building an industry from the top down, Amr Abdelrahim, a researcher at Sciences Po in Paris, reported in a 2024 study. “After 2016, young middle-class musicians and creative professionals, who had been careful to avoid drawing official attention to their countercultural activities suddenly became central to the ambitions of the state,” he wrote.
The careers of young Saudi acts — like Bishi, for example — “became tied to the destiny of the crown prince,” the researcher explained.
The Saudi royal family has long dispersed money from Saudi oil sales to their subjects, in order to ensure economic dependence and loyalty. But, Abdelrahim argued, “what is new about Saudi investments in culture under MBS is an unprecedented degree of centralization and the emergence of new clientelist networks around the country’s de-facto ruler,” using a common abbreviation for Crown Prince Mohammed.
Those involved “are inadvertently participating in the consolidation of the Saudi regime,” he argued.
Observers say a lot of the new music businesses are vague about their ties to the state. But it’s clear they couldn’t work without the state’s financial support and approval.
“Almost all major events are organized by the state or funded by closely linked entities,” a spokesperson from Saudi-focused organization, Alqst for Human Rights, told DW. “This affects the type of music produced, as musicians have to be mindful of what is acceptable. This is not just about the music they produce, but also how they act and what they say to their fans.”
ALQST believes Saudi musicians have even less artistic freedom under the new musical system than before, when they would have played or performed privately. They can lose their contracts and livelihoods, be prevented from performing or even arrested, Alqst’s spokesperson said.
“In the past, the music scene was not regulated,” explained the guitarist and bassist for Saudi black metal band, Al-Namrood. But now that it is, the state can more closely monitor musicians who once stayed hidden and only played privately, the musician, who goes by the name of Mephisto, told DW.
Al-Namrood are one of the rare examples of a Saudi act that isn’t working with state support. The group first formed in 2008 but have never played at home and have kept their identities secret for almost two decades.
“The exchange is clear: You want to perform, it has to be under our rules,” Mephisto continued. “And I totally understand the perspective [of some musicians]. But typically the artist must refrain from any criticism of the religious or authoritarian. [The state] doesn’t necessarily buy an artist’s loyalty, it just creates incentives that make criticism increasingly costly.”
For Al-Namrood, who have often condemned Saudi conservatism, religion and politics in their music, that’s not an option. “We don’t want anything to do with them,” Mephisto said.
In her 2020 paper for the journal, Arabian Humanities, Nora Derbal, a professor at the University of Hamburg, said Saudi artists told her that if they got a call from authorities asking them to participate in a government project, it would be an offer they couldn’t turn down.
The artists she spoke with were debating “their cooptation and loss of autonomy, and about the consequences for not joining in state projects,” she wrote.
On the other hand, in various interviews, Saudi acts who have partaken in their country’s pop music renaissance have also been positive: They don’t have to hide anymore, they can play for larger audiences and they are paid. In an interview, one Saudi DJ described the first Soundstorm festival as like “Berlin after the fall of the wall” while others said they felt they were making history.
“So that’s the interesting paradox,” said Fannie Agerschou-Madsen, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Roskilde in Denmark, who’s written several papers on the topic. “We have all these social liberalizations and challenges to conservative norms but at the same time that’s not being followed by political liberalization.”
But that doesn’t mean that some room isn’t being created for meaningful change, Agerschou-Madsen told DW. Locals told her they enjoyed the newfound freedom of going to a dance party although, she noted, the subversiveness seemed to be more directed at the social conservatism than Saudi authorities.
Young Saudis are well aware of the red lines and state control of the music scene and are continually negotiating boundaries, the researcher argued. In that way, “their everyday practices create space for political and social change, little by little, although perhaps not in what you’d consider a typically revolutionary way.”
So is the Saudi state co-opting local musicians, including those who might have said something controversial before they ever get a chance to?
A DW enquiry to Mdlbeast was not answered. And the answer likely lies somewhere in the middle.
For some young Saudis, the new music scene has been about fun, self-expression, belonging and creativity, Agerschou-Madsen wrote in a new, as-yet-unpublished paper shared with DW. “Others, however, view it as a top-down project that commodifies fun while sidestepping deeper issues of political freedom and social equity.”

item.title: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia’s war on Ukraine
item.description:
Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India’s northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.
But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces.
After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.
In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.
Randhawa’s story is a familiar one in India.
He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.
The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024.
At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.
In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India’s Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.
The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.
The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.
Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. “This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government,” the ministry said.
Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.
“Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation,” Trigunayat told DW.
He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.
“Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents,” Trigunayat said.
The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.
Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine.
He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India.
“Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It’s a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment,” Sufiyan told DW.
Sufiyan’s experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.
Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University’s School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.
“Some of them, they don’t join the army, but they end up in the army region. They’re caught in the crossfire,” Kumar told DW.
He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. “Russia is very cooperative so far,” he said.
India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.
The recruitment efforts reflect Russia’s need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine, and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.
Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin’s need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.
He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.
“In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that,” said Khan.
Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.
“For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable,” he said.

item.title: 11-party alliance to press for July Charter implementation in government dialogue
item.description:
The 11-party alliance will press for implementation of the July Charter and the referendum verdict in the proposed dialogue with the government, insisting that the people's mandate on constitutional reforms must be the central issue in resolving the ongoing political crisis.
Alliance coordinator Hamidur Rahman Azad on Friday said the alliance would also participate in the dialogue as a united platform rather than through its constituent parties separately.
“The issue is not the demand of any particular party; it is a national issue on which political parties have made commitments to the people,” he said.
He made the remarks at a press briefing following a meeting of the 11-party alliance at the party's central Office in the capital.
Hamidur Rahman Azad, also a Jamaat Assistant Secretary General, said around 70 percent of voters had supported 48 constitutional reform proposals in the referendum, with the approved process providing for the formation of a reform council and completion of the reforms within 180 days.
He said the people had already determined the process and timeframe for implementing the reforms, leaving no scope for reopening the fundamental question of how the July Charter should be implemented.
The alliance would finalise its detailed agenda at a meeting of its top leaders before joining the dialogue once the government fixes a date, he added.
Azad said that although cooperation from all sides was necessary to resolve the crisis, the primary responsibility rested with the government.
He also alleged that the government's failure to take steps to implement the July Charter had deepened political divisions.
Meanwhile, the alliance has decided to participate collectively in the Election Commission's dialogue with political parties ahead of the upcoming Union Parishad elections.
Azad said the alliance would formally request the Commission to allocate a separate time slot for all 11 parties instead of inviting them individually.
The liaison committee discussed both the proposed dialogue with the government and the Election Commission's invitation at its meeting, he said.
Azad expressed hope that dialogue and discussions would help resolve the political crisis and fulfil the aspirations of the July mass uprising.

Avengers: Doomsday brings Avengers, X-Men and Fantastic Four together
item.description:
Marvel Studios is bringing together some of its biggest superhero franchises for Avengers: Doomsday, with Robert Downey Jr returning to the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) in an unexpected role as its next major villain, Doctor Doom.
Directed by Joe and Anthony Russo, the film will unite characters from the Avengers, Fantastic Four and X-Men universes in a multiverse conflict. Scheduled to hit theatres on December 18, 2026, the project is being described by Joe Russo as the studio’s most ambitious undertaking yet.
In an extensive cover story published by Entertainment Weekly on November 24, the filmmakers and cast offered new insights into the film, including its scale, character relationships and darker narrative direction.
Downey, who famously portrayed Tony Stark, also known as Iron Man, until the character's death in Avengers: Endgame (2019), will now play Victor von Doom. The return marks a major shift for the actor, who is taking on one of Marvel's most recognisable antagonists.
The story centres on a collapsing multiverse, where incursions bring different realities into collision. The Avengers' world will cross paths with the Fantastic Four and the X-Men, setting up an encounter between characters from previously separate cinematic universes.
The film also brings back Chris Evans as Steve Rogers, alongside Hayley Atwell as Peggy Carter. Pedro Pascal, Vanessa Kirby, Joseph Quinn and Ebon Moss-Bachrach return as members of the Fantastic Four, while familiar X-Men characters include Ian McKellen's Magneto, James Marsden's Cyclops, Rebecca Romijn's Mystique and Alan Cumming's Nightcrawler.
Doctor Doom's character will have a deeper connection to the Fantastic Four, particularly Reed Richards, played by Pascal. The filmmakers revealed that Victor and Reed were close friends during their university years before their paths diverged.
Unlike a conventional superhero antagonist, Doom will also draw on dark magic after experiencing a tragic loss. Anthony Russo described the film's atmosphere as carrying shades of horror, while Downey characterised its story as particularly dark.
Beyond the immediate conflict, Avengers: Doomsday is intended to set the stage for Avengers: Secret Wars, scheduled for December 17, 2027. Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige described the 2 films as a transition from one universe to another, with Secret Wars laying the groundwork for a new phase of MCU storytelling from 2028.
The upcoming crossover represents a significant reunion of characters and franchises that have evolved across decades of Marvel films. With the Russo brothers returning and Downey stepping into a radically different role, Avengers: Doomsday is positioned as a major turning point for the franchise.

item.title: Mosharraf Karim, Sumaiya Shimu reunite for Eid 2027 film ‘Jatra Biroti’
item.description:
Chorki has announced its upcoming theatrical Eid film, Jatra Biroti, starring Mosharraf Karim, Sumaiya Shimu and Prarthana Fardin Dighi. Directed by Kazi Asad, the film is scheduled for release during Eid in 2027.
The story follows a middle-class family on a trip, exploring the laughter, tears, hardships and unexpected incidents they encounter along the way.
Veteran actress Dilara Zaman will play the family's senior member. The cast also includes Yusuf Hasan Arka, Rakib Hossain Evon, Rudra Roy and others.
Shooting is currently underway in Kuakata, with production scheduled to continue through December at various scenic locations.
At 84, Dilara Zaman said she was looking forward to the experience, which would give her an opportunity to travel, spend time with younger colleagues and enjoy herself.
“Otherwise, who would leave home at this age?” she said.
The film also marks the reunion of Mosharraf Karim and Sumaiya Shimu on screen after a long break. It will also mark Shimu's return to cinema following an extended hiatus.
Kazi Asad, who previously directed Chorki's series Adhunik Bangla Hotel and film Lifeline, is making his theatrical directorial debut with the project.
Shimu said the script and her character initially caught her attention, although she was hesitant about joining the project. After discussions with her co-artists and the production house, she eventually decided to come on board.
Mosharraf Karim described working with Shimu again after a long time as a pleasant experience, adding that he was focused on delivering his best performance.
Dighi, who has worked with Shimu and Dilara Zaman since childhood but had never shared the screen with Karim, said she felt slightly nervous about acting alongside him but was excited about the story.
Chorki CEO Redoan Rony said audience enthusiasm for theatrical releases had encouraged the platform to expand its cinema productions through the Chorki Cinema Initiative, describing Jatra Biroti as another step in that direction.
The story was written by Daniel Dany, Kazi Asad and Asaduzzaman Abir, while Asad and Abir jointly wrote the screenplay and dialogues.

item.title: National Film Award winner Matia Banu Shuku passes away
item.description:
National Film Award-winning producer, director and screenwriter Matia Banu Shuku has passed away.
She breathed her last at around 12:05am on Friday after being transferred from the intensive care unit (ICU) to palliative care late Thursday night.
Cultural activist Ershadul Haque Tinku confirmed her death.
According to family sources, her body will be taken to Bakultala on the premises of Dhaka University's Faculty of Fine Arts at 5am, following Fajr prayers.
She will lie in state there until 10:30am to allow people to pay their last respects.
At 11am, her body will be taken to the Central Shaheed Minar for public tributes before being taken to Dhaka University Central Mosque, where her first namaz-e-janaza will be held after Jumma prayers.
She will then be taken to the Uttara Sector 12 Graveyard for burial.
Matia Banu Shuku, the eldest daughter of Language Movement veteran Abdul Matin and wife of filmmaker Nurul Alam Atique, had been suffering from cancer and kidney complications for a long time.

Adulteration threatens date molasses trade in Rajshahi
item.description:
Winter marks the start of date sap collection in rural Rajshahi. Tappers collect date sap early in the morning and boil it to produce the region’s traditional date molasses, prized for its distinctive taste and aroma. However, the centuries-old tradition is now under threat from widespread adulteration.
Instead of using date sap, unscrupulous producers are making molasses by mixing sugar, cane molasses, flour, fabric dyes, chemicals and artificial flavour, then selling it as the genuine product.
Sap collectors said more than 150 factories are producing adulterated molasses in Bagha, Charghat and Puthia upazilas. Each produces 200-300kg a night, while traditional tappers toil all day to make a fraction of that amount, they said.
Rafiqul Islam, a sap collector from Mirganj in Bagha, said: “We struggle to produce even 10kg of molasses, while these factories make five to 10 maunds daily. The administration conducts raids, but the factories reopen the next day. We cannot compete with them.”
Shafiqul Islam, a farmer from Raotha village in Charghat, said artificial flavour makes adulterated molasses smell stronger than the genuine product. He alleged that large wholesalers finance factory owners in advance to secure bulk supplies, leaving genuine producers struggling to get fair prices.
According to Department of Agricultural Extension, Rajshahi has 1,108,018 date trees, concentrated mainly in Bagha, Charghat and Puthia. Bagha alone has around 162,000 trees and 6,060 growers. Nearly 3,000 tappers are involved in sap collection and molasses production during the season.
Baneshwar Bazar in Puthia is one of the region's largest molasses wholesale markets. Market sources estimate that 100-110 tonnes are traded there daily, with volumes rising on the two weekly market days.
Molasses sells for Tk180-200 per kg at the beginning of the season in Bagha, falling to Tk140-160 during the peak season. Wholesalers from Pabna and other districts regularly buy supplies from the markets.
Abul Hossain, a tapper from Chakrajapur char in Bagha, said he leases trees in other areas because there are no date trees in his locality. He has leased 120 trees this season and expects the earnings to support his family for three to four months.
The administration has conducted several drives against adulterated molasses. On November 12 and 15, raids on two factories in Bagha resulted in fines totalling Tk200,000. Earlier drives also led to fines and the seizure and destruction of adulterated molasses and production materials. In Charghat, three traders were fined Tk150,000.
Nusrat Jahan Anannya, assistant commissioner (land) and executive magistrate of Bagha, said fines were imposed for producing molasses in unhygienic conditions using chemicals. The action was taken under Section 41 of Consumer Rights Protection Act, 2009. Seized molasses and ingredients were destroyed publicly, she added.
Charghat Upazila Health Officer Dr Toufiq Reza warned that unauthorized chemicals in molasses could cause diarrhoea and other gastrointestinal problems. Their use in food for children is particularly concerning, he said.
Bagha Upazila Agriculture Officer MA Mannan said government support for commercial production could make the industry more profitable, while exports could unlock further opportunities.
Dr Md Azizur Rahman, additional director of Department of Agricultural Extension in Rajshahi division, said farmers were receiving advice on tree care and increasing production.
The industry offers considerable potential for employment and economic growth, but adulteration threatens public health, genuine producers and the reputation of traditional molasses, he said.

BGB files case over Gopalganj attack, names 5,008 accused
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) has filed a case over an attack on its patrol team in Tungipara, Gopalganj, in which government vehicles were torched, ammunition destroyed, and equipment looted.
Newton Molla, president of the banned Gopalganj District Chhatra League, has been named the prime accused. Seven others have also been named, while 5,000 unidentified people have been listed as accused, bringing the total number of accused to 5,008.
The named accused include Gopalganj District Chhatra League General Secretary Ataur Rahman Pial; former Tungipara upazila Chhatra League General Secretary Babul Hossain Khokon; current upazila Chhatra League President Shamshul Haque; Vice-President Ripon Sheikh; and Joint General Secretary Shahin Biswas, also known as Kalu.
The case was filed at Tungipara Police Station on November 23 following a complaint lodged by Nayeb Subedar Md Shawkat Ali of the BGB's Khulna Sector Headquarters.
Sakhawat Hossain Sentu, additional superintendent of police of Gopalganj's Sadar Circle, confirmed the matter on Thursday night.
According to the First Information Report (FIR), a BGB team was conducting patrols alongside police, Ansar personnel and Executive Magistrate Md Rihab Imam on November 17 to assist the civil administration in maintaining law and order in Gopalganj.
After receiving reports of vandalism and arson at Tungipara Police Station, the team headed towards the area. When they reached Nilfa Bazar in Tungipara, a group of people allegedly blocked the road by felling trees.
The FIR says the BGB personnel asked them to clear the road, but the group attacked them with improvised weapons and detonated crude bombs.
During the attack, a BGB armoured personnel carrier (APC) and a jeep were set on fire. Four BGB personnel — Nayek Md Monir Hossain, Asaduzzaman, Faruk Hossain and Assistant Director Md Saifiar Rahman — were seriously injured while attempting to intervene, according to the complaint.
The FIR states that a BGB Pajero jeep and an APC Cobra were completely destroyed by fire. Three submachine gun (SMG) magazines containing a total of 90 rounds of ammunition inside the jeep were also burnt.
The tyres and fog lights of another APC and the windshield of a pickup truck were damaged. A government-issued laptop, a walkie-talkie set, a battery and a charger kept inside the BGB vehicles were also allegedly looted.
The complaint estimates the total damage at Tk6.51 crore.
ASP Sentu said the case was filed over the attack, arson, vandalism and looting involving BGB personnel and vehicles. No arrests have been made so far, he added.

item.title: Dhaka ranks 5th among world's most polluted cities
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 5th among the world's most polluted cities on Friday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 186 at 9:50am.
The air quality was classified as "unhealthy", meaning the concentration of pollutants in the air had reached a level that could pose health risks to the general population, according to the AQI scale.
According to the AQI ranking, Pakistan's Lahore topped the list with a score of 299, followed by Afghanistan's Kabul with 297 and India'a Delhi and Kolkata with 284 and 231 respectively.
According to AQI standards, a reading between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", while levels above 301 are deemed "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around 7 million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

Trump downplays China and Russia's support to Iran
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran, amid reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target US military bases.
Trump, during a short press conference with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, noted that the Iran conflict had been discussed during his recent trilateral meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
"My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they're very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information," Trump said.
"We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too," he added.
Regarding Russia's intelligence sharing, Trump said: "I don't think they give very much."
He said both countries want to see the conflict with Iran end, and "I think they're helping me in that regard."

National Film Award winner Matia Banu Shuku passes away
item.description:
National Film Award-winning producer, director and screenwriter Matia Banu Shuku has passed away.
She breathed her last at around 12:05am on Friday after being transferred from the intensive care unit (ICU) to palliative care late Thursday night.
Cultural activist Ershadul Haque Tinku confirmed her death.
According to family sources, her body will be taken to Bakultala on the premises of Dhaka University's Faculty of Fine Arts at 5am, following Fajr prayers.
She will lie in state there until 10:30am to allow people to pay their last respects.
At 11am, her body will be taken to the Central Shaheed Minar for public tributes before being taken to Dhaka University Central Mosque, where her first namaz-e-janaza will be held after Jumma prayers.
She will then be taken to the Uttara Sector 12 Graveyard for burial.
Matia Banu Shuku, the eldest daughter of Language Movement veteran Abdul Matin and wife of filmmaker Nurul Alam Atique, had been suffering from cancer and kidney complications for a long time.

item.title: SRB nabs Shibganj blast suspect from Rajshahi hideout
item.description:
A man injured in a crude bomb explosion while allegedly making explosives in Chapainawabganj’s Shibganj has been arrested in Rajshahi.
The arrestee, Nazmul Karim, also known as Nurul, was secretly receiving treatment at a house in Rajshahi city after fleeing the scene of the explosion.
Members of the Special Response Battalion (SRB-5) detained him during a raid on a house in the city’s Tero Khadia Paschimpara area around 8:30pm on Thursday. He was later taken to Rajshahi Medical College Hospital (RMCH) for treatment.
Nazmul hails from Parchouka village in Shibganj upazila. He runs a tea stall in the area and is locally known as a crude bomb maker. SRB-5 claimed that he is an activist of the activities-banned Awami League.
At the time of the raid, Nazmul was receiving an intravenous saline infusion. SRB personnel took him to the hospital in their ambulance, along with his wife and a female tenant of the house.
According to police and local sources, an explosion occurred around noon on Wednesday while cocktails were being made in Parchouka village. Thomas Ali was killed on the spot.
Thomas was the personal assistant to former Awami League lawmaker Dr Samil Uddin Ahmed Shimul, who represented the Chapainawabganj-1 (Shibganj) constituency.
He was the son of Md Mortuza of Bishwanathpur Lambar Tola village in the upazila. On his Facebook profile, Thomas identified himself as a member of the Shibganj upazila unit of the Krishak League and an Awami League activist. His profile also featured photographs of him attending various Awami League programmes.
Three others injured in the explosion fled the scene, including Nazmul. He initially received treatment at a private clinic in Rajshahi before taking shelter at a rented house in Tero Khadia Paschimpara belonging to a woman known to him.
The house is owned by Md Alauddin, a retired professor of the English Department at Rajshahi College.
A female tenant of the house, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Nazmul was previously known to them. His wife brought him to the house on Wednesday after he received treatment at the clinic.
They had planned to return to their village home on Thursday after having his wounds dressed, she said. However, an unidentified man arrived around noon and administered saline to Nazmul. SRB personnel surrounded the house later that evening.
The woman said she did not know how Nazmul had been injured. However, during his stay, he told her that he had been at the scene of the explosion and had been taken there on a motorcycle.
SRB-5 Commanding Officer Lieutenant Colonel Md Foysal Istiaq said Nazmul was the only person detained from the house.
He said Nazmul was taken to RMCH as he required medical attention and would remain under police custody while receiving treatment.
He added that Nazmul would be shown arrested in the case filed over the explosion and produced before a court after recovering.

item.title: BADC chairman stresses transparency, accountability in implementing development plans
item.description:
Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) held a farewell program for its Chairman Md Azizul Islam at the conference room of the corporation’s headquarters at Krishi Bhaban on Thursday following his transfer.
Heads of all wings and divisions, representatives of professional organizations, and officials from different levels attended the program, said a press release.
Speaking at the event, Azizul Islam said BADC was one of the country's oldest and most traditional institutions, with a vital role in agriculture and agricultural production.
He said the corporation had earned farmers' trust by ensuring the effective delivery of essential agricultural inputs and services, including quality seeds, non-urea fertilizers, and irrigation facilities, to farmers' doorsteps.
He also noted that the scope of the corporation's activities had been expanding over the years. Implementing annual work plans with less than half of its approved workforce was both a major challenge and a significant achievement, he added.
Highlighting key initiatives, he stressed the need to ensure the timely supply of fertilizers, excavate and re-excavate canals, and implement measures to achieve self-sufficiency in onion and jute seed production for the first time.

item.title: Alif Paribahan bus catches fire in Uttar Badda
item.description:

Two Fire Service units rushed to the scene and brought the blaze under control.
The Fire Service received the report of the fire at 9:50pm on Thursday.
Fire Service Duty Officer Rafi Al Faruk said two units responded to the incident and brought the fire under control at around 10:30pm.
He said the cause of the fire could not be immediately determined.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,371 as 8 die in 24 hours
item.description:
The measles outbreak has claimed 8 more lives in Bangladesh in the 24 hours up to 8am on Thursday, taking the total death toll from confirmed cases and suspected measles to 1,371 since March 15, 2026.
Of the latest fatalities, 7 were reported among children with measles-like symptoms, while 1 was from a confirmed measles case, according to a press release issued by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) on Thursday.
The DGHS recorded 1,109 suspected and confirmed measles cases during the same period.
With the latest fatalities, the death toll from suspected measles reached 1,265 since March 15. Meanwhile, deaths from confirmed measles cases stood at 106, including 1 reported in the 24 hours up to 8am on Thursday.
According to the release, 1,007 suspected measles cases were reported during the latest 24-hour period, taking the total to 261,535 since March 15.
Another 102 confirmed cases were reported during the same period, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to 26,476.
Between March 15 and November 26, a total of 234,280 patients with suspected measles were admitted to hospitals across the country. Of them, 225,568 were discharged, the release added.

item.title: PM eyes export-led growth in livestock sector
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has called for transforming Bangladesh’s livestock sector into a modern, self-reliant and export-oriented industry, pledging policy and financial support to increase production, ensure food security and expand overseas markets.
Addressing the National Livestock Week-2026 at the old Trade Fair ground in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar on Thursday, he said agriculture, fisheries and livestock were central to the rural economy, contributing to nutrition, employment, poverty reduction and economic growth.
“If we can meet our nutritional needs through domestic production and transform that production into an industry, building a self-reliant and prosperous economy will not be difficult,” he said, stressing proper planning and effective implementation.
The livestock sector contributes 1.81% to Bangladesh’s GDP at constant prices in the current fiscal year and accounts for 16.56% of agricultural GDP, with a growth rate of 3.30%, according to the prime minister.
Between March and August 2026, the country earned $10.464 million from livestock-related exports. Tarique said there was significant potential to expand exports of leather goods, animal by-products, processed foods, halal meat, dairy and poultry products. Bangladesh has also recently developed the capacity to commercially export fertile hatching eggs.
The prime minister said the government was prioritising improved livestock breeds, artificial insemination, vaccination, disease prevention, modern feed management and waste management to make the sector more productive.
Bangladesh has more than 200,000 commercial and small-scale poultry farms, producing around 6.88 crore eggs daily. The industry employs about six million people, 40% of them women, and has attracted nearly Tk50,000 crore in private investment, he said. Around 1.5 million marginal farmers also depend on livestock for their livelihoods.
Identifying animal diseases as a major challenge, Tarique said existing research institutions produce vaccines against 17 diseases, but capacity remains inadequate. The government has taken an initiative to establish a modern vaccine production plant to strengthen disease prevention and veterinary services.
Tarique called for exploring buffalo farming in coastal areas and the haor regions of Sylhet and Sunamganj. He urged the Land Ministry to work with the Fisheries and Livestock Ministry and local administrations to allocate newly emerged coastal char land and government-owned khas land to farmers through cooperatives.
He also pledged training, affordable loans, modern technology and fair prices for farmers, saying their contribution was central to the sector’s development.
The prime minister stressed protecting animals from hunger, disease, pain and distress, and ensuring they can express natural behaviour. “Just as humans have rights, the rights of animals and birds must not be overlooked,” he said.
He also underscored the need to meet international food safety and quarantine standards, saying the government was working to establish modern processing centres and disease-free zones to improve access to overseas markets.
Congratulating recipients of the National Livestock Award-2026, Tarique expressed confidence that Bangladesh could become a trusted global brand in livestock products and a major source of foreign exchange earnings.

item.title: Clash between police, workers in Gazipur; ASP injured
item.description:
A clash broke out between garment workers and police in Sreepur, Gazipur, on Thursday as workers blocked the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway in protest.
Several police personnel, including Additional Superintendent of Police (ASP) Md Shafiqul Islam of the Gazipur District Police's Kaliakair Circle, were injured.
The incident occurred around 11am in the Nayanpur area of Sreepur upazila.
According to police and eyewitnesses, workers from several nearby factories gathered in a procession and occupied part of the Dhaka-Mymensingh highway, bringing traffic to a standstill.
Police moved to clear the road and restore traffic, firing tear gas shells and sound grenades to disperse the workers. During the confrontation, workers allegedly threw bricks at police, injuring ASP Shafiqul Islam and several other police personnel.
The situation has since stabilised, and traffic on the highway has returned to normal.
Md Nahid Niyaz Shishir, assistant commissioner (land) and executive magistrate of Sreepur upazila, confirmed the incident. He said law enforcement personnel intervened after workers blocked the highway around 11am, using tear gas to clear the road and restore traffic. He also confirmed that several police officers and personnel were injured by bricks thrown during the clash.
Meanwhile, amid the ongoing unrest, factories in several areas, including Konabari and Palli Bidyut in Gazipur, declared fresh closures on Thursday.
Factories in Bagher Bazar and Bhabanipur in Gazipur Sadar upazila, as well as Gargarhia Masterbari, Bairagir Chala and Kew in Sreepur upazila, have also announced a three-day holiday.
Law enforcement personnel remain on high alert at key points along the Dhaka-Tangail highway to prevent further incidents.

item.title: Bangladesh to Host Inaugural Impact Investment Day on Dec 2-3
item.description:
Bangladesh will hold its first Impact Investment Day on December 2 and 3 in Dhaka, bringing together investors, regulators, intermediaries and impact entrepreneurs to explore how local capital can drive social and environmental progress.
Titled Impact InvesTIME 2026, the two-day summit will run under the theme "Mobilizing Domestic Capital."
It is organized by the National Advisory Board (NAB) for Impact Investment in Bangladesh in collaboration with GSG Impact and partners, convening more than 60 speakers-- including 18 from overseas across 14 countries -- alongside leaders from domestic and global impact investment ecosystems.
NAB unveiled the program at a press conference at its headquarters in Dhaka on Thursday.
At the briefing, NAB Bangladesh CEO Farhadur Reza outlined the country's impact investment landscape and the guidance the summit aims to deliver.
Speakers noted that as Bangladesh prepares to transition toward upper-middle-income status and faces declining reliance on concessional foreign aid in the years ahead, mobilizing domestic capital is becoming increasingly vital.
According to the organizers, Bangladesh holds substantial pools of savings, banking assets, pension and insurance funds, Islamic finance and diaspora remittances that could be directed into investments generating financial returns alongside measurable social and environmental outcomes.
Local capital has already backed small and medium enterprises, climate resilience, women's entrepreneurship and job creation, and the summit will focus on scaling those efforts.
During the press briefing, Zayad Al Ibrahim, representing NAB member organization ActionAid, explained the distinction between conventional investment and impact investment.
Answering questions from journalists, Build Bangladesh director Erad Kawsar said Bangladesh holds strong potential to achieve social, economic and environmental development through impact investment powered by domestic capital.
The opening day will begin with speeches and keynote addresses, followed by the launch of StartUpwards, an exhibition showcasing impact startups and entrepreneurs.
The schedule also features panels on ecosystem enablers and local entrepreneurs' achievements, a celebration of the Global Change Award, a regional discussion on financing the impact economy, and a formal dinner.
Day two will examine risk and private capital, impact transparency and measurement, and government support for the impact economy, alongside parallel sessions and interactive workshops for investment stakeholders.
NAB will also present the Impact InveSTAR recognition to impact leaders.
Delegates and speakers from Australia, India, Indonesia, Japan, the Netherlands, Spain, Sri Lanka and Switzerland are expected to join Bangladeshi participants, with representatives from Sri Lanka, India, Indonesia and Australia appearing on a South-South regional collaboration panel.
Plans also include business school master classes and one-to-one meetings connecting overseas delegates with regulators, entrepreneurs and financial institutions.
NAB has worked to build Bangladesh's impact investment ecosystem since 2018, with its secretariat hosted by Build Bangladesh.
Partners to date include GSG Impact, GSG Japan, Build Bangladesh, Impact Investing Australia, Jica, Swiss Contact, the Embassy of Switzerland, BRAC, UCB Bank, Sajida Foundation, ANDE, the Bangladesh Institute of Capital Market, North South University and Impress Capital Limited, as well as NAB chapters in Australia, Sri Lanka, India and Indonesia.

item.title: Nestlé Bangladesh, Singer Bangladesh sign strategic partnership
item.description:
Nestlé Bangladesh and Singer Bangladesh have signed a strategic partnership to promote convenient home cooking through a collaboration between Singer's kitchen appliances and Nestlé's MAGGI brand.
The partnership was formalized through a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on November 24.
The MoU was signed by Deepal Abeywickrema, chairman and managing director of Nestlé Bangladesh PLC, and M H M Fairoz, managing director of Singer Bangladesh.
Shammi Rubayet Karim, head of communication and marketing services at Nestlé Bangladesh, and Bedoura Farhana, head of marketing at Singer Bangladesh, were also present, along with senior officials from both companies.
The collaboration aims to combine Singer's kitchen appliances with MAGGI's recipes to offer Bangladeshi consumers convenient and enjoyable home-cooking experiences.
The partnership brings together the 2 brands and is intended to pave the way for future joint innovations tailored to the evolving lifestyles of Bangladeshi households.

item.title: Wage board to hold fifth meeting on Thursday
item.description:
The wage board is scheduled to hold its fifth meeting on Thursday to finalise the minimum wage for workers and employees in the ready-made garment (RMG) sector.
The meeting will begin at 11:30am in Segunbagicha, Dhaka, chaired by Wage Board Chairman and District and Sessions Judge Syed Azad Subhani.
At its fourth meeting, held last Tuesday, the board proposed setting the minimum wage for garment workers at Tk17,000, up from the current Tk12,500. If implemented, the proposal would mean an increase of Tk4,500.
The board members also unanimously agreed on proposed wage structures for three grades. Under the proposal, the minimum wage for Grade 1 workers has been set at Tk21,500, while Grade 2 and Grade 3 workers would receive Tk20,000 and Tk19,200, respectively.
The wage board was formed to make recommendations on minimum wages for workers and employees across different categories in the garment industry.

item.title: Ruposhi Bangla Express suspension disrupts Benapole-Dhaka passengers
item.description:
Bangladesh Railway has temporarily suspended the Ruposhi Bangla Express on the Benapole-Dhaka route on security grounds, causing inconvenience to passengers, while the scheduled journey of the Jahanabad Express on the Khulna-Dhaka route has also been cancelled.
However, the Jahanabad Express will operate on an alternative route.
Benapole Railway Station Master Parvina Khatun said Bangladesh Railway had issued a notice announcing the cancellation of the scheduled services of trains Ruposhi Bangla Express and Jahanabad Express on Thursday.
According to the notice, the decision was taken in the interest of overall railway security as the railway authorities had not received specific opinions or information from the relevant local administration in Gopalganj district regarding the safe operation of trains.
Jessore Railway Station Master Saidur Rahman said the Ruposhi Bangla Express on the Benapole-Jessore-Dhaka route and the Jahanabad Express on the Khulna-Dhaka route had been temporarily suspended.
However, the Jahanabad Express would continue operating via an alternative route, he added. According to railway sources, the alternative service of the Jahanabad Express will operate on the Khulna-Poradaha-Rajbari-Dhaka route.
The train will leave Dhaka at 4:10pm and reach Khulna at 11:35pm. In the opposite direction, it will depart Khulna at 8:00am and arrive in Dhaka at 3:10pm.
The alternative train will stop at Daulatpur, Noapara, jessore, Mobarakganj, Kotchandpur and Darshana. It will also make scheduled stops at Chuadanga, Alamdanga, Poradaha, Kushtia Court, Kumarkhali, Pangsha, Rajbari, Faridpur and Bhanga.
With the suspension of the direct train service, passengers are facing additional travel expenses. Day and night coach fares from Benapole to Dhaka range between Tk 1,500 and Tk 1,800, while train fares from Benapole were Tk 889 for AC, Tk 460 for non-AC and Tk 960 for a cabin, according to the information provided.
Benapole businessman Babulur Rahman said he had bought a ticket before November 19 to travel to Dhaka but had yet to receive a refund following the suspension of the train service.
Aynal Haque, another station master at Benapole Railway Station, said the Ruposhi Bangla Express had remained suspended on the Benapole-Dhaka route since November 19.
He said the process of refunding ticket prices to passengers was underway, but the authorities had not officially announced when the train service would resume.

item.title: PM inaugurates zero-cost manpower export to Malaysia
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday inaugurated the country's first government-initiated programme to send workers to Malaysia entirely free of costs.
He also saw 112 Bangladeshi workers off on the first flight under the scheme at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, his Assistant Press Secretary Gazi Shahriar Pamir said.
Tarique Rahman thanked the Malaysian government for creating employment opportunities for Bangladeshi workers.
The initiative comes after Malaysia's labour market reopened to Bangladeshi workers following a gap of two and a half years.
The workers were selected through Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) from 4,039 applicants, based on a public e-lottery and direct interview by the employer.
They will work for DHL Supply Chain in Malaysia on a three-year renewable contract at a monthly basic salary of 1,700 Malaysian ringgit (MYR). The employer will also provide accommodation and medical facilities. The recruiting company is bearing all migration-related expenses of the workers.
Another 225 Bangladeshi workers are scheduled to go to Malaysia at no cost in December under the programme. BOESL has so far received attested demand letters for 1,048 workers from four Malaysian companies.
Labour and Employment and Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury, Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat, Prime Minister’s Adviser Mahdi Amin, State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Md Nurul Hoque, Special Assistants to the Prime Minister Dr Md Shakirul Islam Khan and Barrister Gias Uddin Rimon, and Dhaka-18 MP SM Jahangir Hossain, among others, were present on the occasion.
BOESL Managing Director Mohammad Rashedul Haque, DHL Supply Chain Malaysia Managing Director Debarshi Majumdar, General Manager Navinder Murugiah, partner Saravanakumar Kanesan, and Abdul Jalil, regional recruitment director at Seremban Suria in Malaysia, were also present, along with senior officials of the ministries and agencies concerned.
After assuming office in February, Tarique Rahman made his first foreign visit to Malaysia in June this year.
At a bilateral meeting with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim in Putrajaya on June 22, he called for an early reopening of the labour market for Bangladeshi workers and the recruitment of more workers.
The two leaders agreed at the meeting to reduce migration costs and make the recruitment process transparent, fair and affordable.

item.title: BSU protests removal of Professor Snigdha as JU provost
item.description:
The Jahangirnagar University (JU) unit of Bangladesh Student Union (BSU) has condemned the removal of Professor Rejwana Karim Snigdha from her position as provost of Begum Sufia Kamal Hall, alleging that a politically motivated smear campaign and cyberbullying led to the decision.
In a joint statement issued on Thursday, the organisation’s President Adree Ankur and General Secretary Faizan Ahmed Orko said the campaign against the Anthropology Department professor was part of a broader attempt to undermine democratic space at the university and politically marginalize teachers holding dissenting views.
They said coordinated social media campaigns were being used to spread hatred against the professor, undermining not only her personal dignity but also freedom of expression, independent thinking and democratic culture on campus.
The student leaders alleged that Professor Snigdha had been politically labelled and subjected to public vilification without any proper and impartial institutional investigation into the allegations against her.
They also rejected the practice of branding individuals as guilty through the media and social media based on allegations of being collaborators of the previous Awami League government or their political affiliations.
The statement criticised the university administration for allegedly failing to ensure impartial and transparent accountability for those who benefited from the power structure during the Awami League regime, collaborated in repression or were involved in curtailing democratic rights.
The leaders also questioned the appointment of several teachers who allegedly benefited from the previous regime to administrative positions after the July Mass Uprising.
Highlighting Professor Snigdha's role in various movements, the statement said she had actively participated in the anti-Hasina movement, protests against the university's master plan, the 2024 anti-rape movement and different stages of the July Mass Uprising.
Ignoring her history of activism and political positions while portraying her through a reactionary political narrative amounted to a distortion of history, they said.
The student leaders also expressed concern over what they described as the growing influence of reactionary social forces in different spheres following the July uprising.
They said public anger and political emotions should not be used to justify extrajudicial social punishment, character assassination or interference in administrative decisions.
Removing a teacher from an administrative position under political pressure without investigating the allegations against them reflects a decline in administrative independence, institutional accountability and democratic values, the statement said.
The Student Union said universities must not become subordinate to political groups, fundamentalist forces or vested interests. Instead, they should remain open spaces for free thought, rationalism, scientific outlook, democratic practices and progressive politics.
Protecting that space is not simply a matter of supporting an individual but a question of safeguarding the democratic character of the university, the statement added.

item.title: Gold worth Tk1.15cr seized from 8 passengers at Sylhet airport
item.description:
Joint teams of National Security Intelligence (NSI) and customs seized 681 grams of raw 24-karat gold valued at Tk1.15 crore from eight passengers at Sylhet Osmani International Airport on Thursday morning.
The seizure took place around 10am aboard Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight BG-236 arriving from Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
Customs sources estimated the market value of the seized gold at Tk1,15,53,000. Subsequently, Tk2,91,926 was realized in revenue against the seized gold.
NSI and customs conducted the joint drive based on secret information as part of heightened intelligence surveillance to prevent duty evasion at the airport.
Osmani International Airport Director Mahmud Akhter Hossain said customs authorities have not yet formally informed the airport administration about the drive.
